# <span style="display:none">Constructors and Constructor Overloading</span>

## Constructors and Constructor Overloading

<!-- Slide 7 -->

---

## Why Use a Constructor?

If every object must be initialized with a separate setter call, are we making the client do too much work?

<!-- Slide 8 -->

---

## Constructors

![](images/source_pages/slide-27.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Constructors"}

<!-- Slide 9 -->

---

## Over and Over

The repeated pattern is object creation followed by a setter call. A constructor moves that initialization into the object-creation step.

<!-- Slide 10 -->

---

## Constructor Defined

A constructor is a special member function with the same name as its class and no return type. It runs automatically when an object is instantiated.

<!-- Slide 11 -->

---

## Constructor Example

```{.cpp}
class Date {
public:
    Date(int month, int day, int year);
};

Date date(10, 15, 2009);
```

<!-- Slide 12 -->

---

## Constructor Output

```text
Date date(10, 15, 2009);
The constructor receives the arguments and initializes the object.
```

## What If There Is More Than One Initialization Path?

What if a class needs more than one way to initialize an object?

<!-- Slide 18 -->

---

## Constructor Overloading Visualization

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**One class**

`Sale()`

`Sale(0.06)`

`Sale(0.06, 24.95)`
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Each constructor signature is an entry path to the same class. The compiler selects the matching constructor from the arguments supplied at instantiation.
:::
:::

## Expected Output

```text
With a 0.06 sale tax rate, the total of the $24.95 sale is $26.45
On a tax-exempt sale, the total of the $24.95 sale is $24.95
```
